ALLEMANDS: In 1917, Germany, an ally of the Central Powers, weakened Tsarist Russia through its offensives.
Wilhelm II, a sworn enemy of the Bolsheviks, symbolized for Lenin the imperialism that had to be defeated in Europe.
The Russian bourgeoisie hoped that Wilhelm II would restore order in a country in the midst of revolution.
occupied Ukraine and the Baltic countries, plundering their resources to starve revolutionary Russia.
Its troops, supposedly sent to crush the revolution, were influenced by Bolshevik agitation in 1918.
The Kaiser's army saw its soldiers fraternize with Russian workers in occupied territory.
The humiliating German peace terms accelerated the radicalization of the Bolsheviks in 1918.
Its soldiers, exposed to revolutionary ideas, formed their own Soviets after November 1918.
For Lenin, Wilhelm II was a “crowned bandit,” an enemy of the worldwide proletarian revolution.
The collapse of the front in 1918 was partly caused by the influence of Russian revolutionaries
AMERICAINS_DU_NORD: In 1917, the United States, a model of democracy, entered the war against the Russian Revolution.
Wilson, hostile to the Bolsheviks, sent troops to Russia to crush the Soviet Republic.
The Americans financed Kolchak and the Whites, fearing the spread of revolution in Europe.
The American Red Cross served as a cover to spy on and arm the enemies of the Bolsheviks.
US soldiers landed in Vladivostok and Arkhangelsk, at the heart of the anti-Red intervention.
John Reed, an American journalist, celebrated the revolution in "Ten Days That Shook the World".
For Lenin, the US plutocracy, despite its democracy, saw Soviet Russia as a mortal danger.
American workers fighting in Goldfield inspired Russian revolutionaries in 1917.
US troops, sent against the Reds, feared being influenced by their ideas.
The United States, an imperialist power, wanted to stifle socialism and control Siberia.
BLANCS_BIELORUSSES: The Belarusian Rada, created in 1917, united the bourgeoisie and kulaks against the Soviets.
Belarusian nationalists allied themselves with the Poles and Germans to crush the revolution.
Under the guise of independence, the Rada prepared an armed uprising against the Bolsheviks.
Wealthy Belarusian peasants formed militias, supported by Dovbor-Musnitsky and his Poles.
The All-Belarusian Congress rejected the Soviets, advocating a bourgeois state under foreign protection.
The White Belarusians fled before the Red Army, seeking help from the Entente in 1918.
The Rada, hostile to the Soviets, collaborated with the German occupiers to preserve its power.
The Belarusian nationalists, anti-Soviet, relied on foreign powers to crush the Reds.
The Belarusian Rada attempted to separate Belarus from Soviet Russia
The Rada used the rhetoric of autonomy to mobilize support but allied itself with the imperialist powers
BLANCS_FINLANDAIS: In 1917, the Finnish bourgeoisie refused to help Petrograd and prepared for independence.
The Finnish Senate proclaimed independence in 1917, but then turned against the Soviets.
Svinhufvud, overthrown by the Reds, called on Germany to crush the Finnish Revolution.
German troops restored the Finnish bourgeoisie to power, unleashing a bloody terror.
In May 1918, thousands of Finnish revolutionaries were executed by the Whites.
Bourgeois Finland became an Entente base for attacking Soviet Russia.
The United States financed the White Finns, turning them into a bulwark against Bolshevism.
Despite independence, Moscow retained the Ino base to defend socialist interests in the Baltic.
The White Finns, allied with the imperialists, crushed the Reds with extreme violence.
Finland, freed from the Russians, became a counter-revolutionary stronghold in Northern Europe.
BLANCS_UKRAINIENS: The Kiev Rada, bourgeois and nationalist, refused orders from Petrograd as early as 1917.
The White Ukrainians blocked grain trains bound for Petrograd, starving the Red cities.
The Rada formed a national army, extending its territory as far as the Urals against Moscow.
Petlyura and Vinnichenko allied themselves with Germany to crush the Soviets in Ukraine.
Kiev disarmed the Red Guards and sabotaged revolutionary reinforcements heading toward the Don.
The Rada signed Brest-Litovsk, handing Ukrainian grain over to the Germans in exchange for bayonets.
The Entente financed the Rada, seeing Ukraine as a springboard against Soviet Russia.
The White Ukrainians, anti-Soviet, dreamed of a “united Russia”… without Bolsheviks.
The Donbas, a Red stronghold, resisted the Rada and its imperialist allies in 1918.
France, the UK and the USA provided loans and military missions to Ukraine as a base for aggression against Russia
BRITANNIQUES_DU_CAUCASE: London wanted to force Russia to repay its Tsarist debts, even after 1917.
The British feared Bolshevik "contagion," a threat to their colonial empire.
The United Kingdom financed Kolchak and Denikin, betting on their victory over the Reds.
Ten thousand British soldiers landed in Arkhangelsk to crush the Russian Revolution.
The Lockhart Mission organized plots against Lenin, with the help of the Red Cross.
London occupied Baku and Vladivostok, seeking to control oil and Siberia.
The British press demonized the Bolsheviks, justifying armed intervention in Russia.
British sailors sympathetic to the Reds refused to fight the Soviets in 1919.
Workers' Councils of Action threatened strikes if London attacked Petrograd.
The British failure in Russia pushed London to lift the blockade and negotiate with Moscow.

FRANCAIS_DU_SUD: France took part in the Entente effort to stifle the Russian Revolution.
It wanted to recover the debts of the Tsarist regime through arms sales.
Soviet Russia was seen as an ideological threat that had to be eliminated.
France targeted the resources of the Caucasus and Ukraine (coal, iron).
It financially and militarily supported the White Armies (Kolchak, Denikin).
French troops landed in Odessa, Sevastopol and Vladivostok.
France used the Czechoslovak Corps as a vanguard against the Bolsheviks.
French workers went on strike to block the shipment of weapons to the White Armies.
Jeanne Labourbe, a French Bolshevik executed by firing squad in Odessa, became a symbol of workers' resistance.
French soldiers mutinied, refusing to fight the Bolsheviks in the Black Sea.
JAPONAIS: Japan carried out an armed intervention in Russia to stifle the Revolution.
It sought to annex Siberia and the Russian Far East as far as the Urals.
Lenin described the Japanese as “marauders” because of their looting.
Japan landed at Khabarovsk on April 5, 1918, after a provocation.
Vladivostok became the main base of the Allied interventionist forces.
Japan supported the counter-revolutionaries Semyonov and Kalmykov with weapons and funds.
Japanese General Otani commanded the interventionist troops in Siberia in 1918.
The Soviets prepared retreats and railway sabotage.
Lenin exploited the Japan–United States rivalry to weaken their intervention.
Japan withdrew from the Russian Far East in late 1922 after a series of failures.
KERENSKI: Kerensky was the head of the government overthrown in November 1917
Kerensky fled Petrograd on November 7 to organize an anti-Bolshevik counterattack.
Kerensky and his remaining troops would be defeated at Pulkovo
The Cossacks refused to continue fighting, declaring that they did not want to fight all of Russia.
The death battalions, created by Kerensky, were ultra-patriotic.
The Red Guards and sailors of Kronstadt crushed Kerensky's offensive.
The Junkers mutinied in Petrograd but were defeated on November 11.
The Junkers, officer cadets, formed the core of Kerensky's troops.
The Don Cossacks were his main anti-Bolshevik armed force.
The Don Cossacks were his main anti-Bolshevik armed force.
LEGION_TCHEQUE: The Czech Legion was a spearhead of the anti-Bolshevik struggle in 1918.
It was formed from Austrian prisoners and deserters after February 1917.
It numbered 25,000 men in August 1917 and was supported by the Entente.
Masaryk helped organize this corps to fight the revolution.
According to Kornilov's plan, the Czechs were to attack Petrograd.
Their armed revolt broke out in May 1918, violating an agreement with the Soviets.
The Entente financed them to destroy the Bolshevik government.
They occupied the Volga region, the Urals and Siberia, taking Samara and Omsk.
12,000 Czechs joined the Red Army against their leaders.
Defeated with Kolchak in late 1919, their defeat marked an imperialist failure.
POLONAIS: Poland was a key instrument of the Entente against Soviet Russia.
The Polish Corps, led by Dovbor-Musnitsky, numbered 25,000 men.
The Entente financed and armed Polish units to fight the Bolsheviks.
France used Poland as a “battering ram” against the Soviet Republic.
Poland attacked Russia in 1920, capturing Kiev to expand its territory.
The Bolsheviks proposed peace, but Poland refused, seeing it as a sign of weakness.
The Red Army pushed the Poles back to the gates of Warsaw in 1920.
Polish workers demonstrated against their government's imperialist war.
Demoralized Polish soldiers often refused to fight the Red Army.
Lenin stated that the Poles wanted peace, not economic war.
BLANCS_DENIKINE: Denikin led the Volunteer Army, the main force of the Russian counter-revolution.
His army was created after the failure of General Kornilov's revolt.
Officers formed the core of his troops, which were well trained and disciplined.
The Don, Kuban and Terek Cossacks supported Denikin out of fear of agrarian reforms.
Kaledin, a Cossack leader, was a key ally of Denikin against the Bolsheviks.
The Cadets, Mensheviks and Right SRs supported Denikin under the guise of "democracy".
The Entente (UK, France, USA) armed and financed Denikin with weapons and money.
Denikin used rapid raids to spread panic in Soviet-controlled areas.
The Red Army crushed Denikin near Tsaritsyn, inflicting 30,000 casualties.
His defeat marked the failure of the White forces on the Southern Front in 1919.
BLANCS_KOLTCHACK: Kolchak, a Tsarist admiral, proclaimed himself Supreme Ruler of Russia in Siberia.
His regime sought to restore the power of capitalists and landowners.
His troops included officers, bourgeois elements and anti-Bolshevik Cossacks.
Kolchak was financed and armed by France, Great Britain and the United States.
He collaborated with the Japanese, rivals of the Americans in Siberia against the Soviets.
His 1919 offensive threatened the Volga, creating a major danger for the Bolsheviks.
His regime imposed a military dictatorship, executing thousands of workers and peasants.
The Mensheviks and SRs supported his White governments in Samara and Omsk.
The peasants and workers of Siberia rose up, causing the collapse of his armies.
Captured in 1920, Kolchak was executed, marking the end of the White generals.
BLANCS_IOUDENITCH: Yudenich led the White forces against Petrograd, supported by the Entente.
Churchill organized the attack to quickly crush Soviet Russia.
Great Britain equipped and landed thousands of White Guards.
His troops included former Russian prisoners trained in England.
Yudenich launched a surprise attack from Estonia, taking advantage of the negotiations.
He captured Krasnoye Selo, Gatchina and Vyritsa to isolate Petrograd.
His plan: cut the railways to starve Petrograd and force it into submission.
The Red Army mobilized 30,000 workers from Petrograd to oppose him.
His defeat marked the third major Soviet success against the Whites.
Yudenich's failure led the Entente to use Poland against the Soviets.
BLANCS_BASMATCHI: The Basmachi movement was a counter-revolution in Central Asia against the Soviets.
It brought together feudal elites, bourgeois elements, Tsarist officers and local nationalists.
Shuro-Islamia and Uleme led the Uzbek and Muslim nationalist bourgeoisie.
The "Kokand Government" proclaimed the autonomy of Turkestan in 1917.
The Basmachi attacked Tashkent with armed nationalist detachments.
The British armed the Basmachi and coordinated their actions.
The White Cossacks and the Khan of Khiva supported the Basmachi.
The Ittifaki, workers and poor peasants, supported the local Bolsheviks.
The Red Guards liberated Kokand in February 1918, crushing the Basmachi.
Their defeat prevented the bourgeoisie from attacking Tashkent and consolidated Soviet power.
ANARCHISTES_KRONSTAD: Kronstadt was a revolutionary stronghold in 1917, supported by its sailors.
The anarchists rejected the centralized state and opposed the Bolshevik dictatorship.
Lenin criticized the anarchists as “petty-bourgeois phrase-mongers.”
In 1921, the slogan “Soviets without Bolsheviks” gained ground in Kronstadt.
They demanded complete freedom of the press, which the Bolsheviks refused.
The Bolsheviks saw bourgeois newspapers as counter-revolutionary weapons.
The anarchist opposition defended “freedom of trade” against the proletarian state.
Their revolt reflected fear of Bolshevik discipline and centralization.
The Bolsheviks feared a return to capitalism through their demands.
The revolt was crushed by the Red Army in March 1921.
BLANCS_MAKHNOVCHTCHINA: The Makhnovshchina was a Ukrainian anarchist movement led by Nestor Makhno.
It was regarded as a petty-bourgeois counter-revolutionary force in Ukraine.
Makhno symbolized anarchy and banditry, more dangerous than the White generals.
His movement relied on armed peasants who elected their own local leaders.
The Makhnovists acted without discipline, rejecting any central Soviet authority.
Their slogan: “I take everything; the others can go hang themselves.”
They created extreme chaos, disrupting logistics and harvests.
The Red Army had to intensify its attacks to crush their armed bands.
The peasants, tired of the excesses, eventually supported the Soviets against Makhno.
Makhno was definitively defeated after Wrangel's defeat in 1920.
BLANCS_PAYSANS_VERT: The Russian peasantry represented 80% of the population and was politically divided.
The kulaks, wealthy peasants, led the resistance against the Bolsheviks.
They rejected grain requisitions and the Soviet monopoly.
Their slogan: “Unlimited freedom of trade” in order to sell grain at high prices.
The Bolsheviks saw this demand as a return to capitalism.
The SRs and Mensheviks supported the kulaks against Soviet power.
Kulak mutinies coincided with the offensives of the White armies.
The “Green Movement” brought together peasants fleeing conscription.
These “Green bands” avoided the Civil War without a clear ideology.
The Red Army crushed both organized and spontaneous peasant resistance.
BLANCS_BALTES: The Baltic countries underwent Russification under the Tsars and the Provisional Government.
The Bolsheviks recognized their right to self-determination after October 1917.
The bourgeois Baltic National Councils rejected autonomy within Russia.
The Latvian Riflemen, 40,000 strong, overwhelmingly supported the Bolsheviks.
Between 70 and 76% of rural Baltic Soviets voted Bolshevik in 1917.
The Latvians resisted the Germans and supported Petrograd against Yudenich.
The Bolsheviks confiscated the lands of the German barons in Latvia.
The Baltic National Councils, together with the Cadets and Mensheviks, led the counter-revolution.
The Entente used the Baltic countries as a rear base against the Soviets.
The Soviet peace treaty with Estonia marked a diplomatic victory in 1920.
